The night sky is a terrible liar. It pretends to be still, a painted ceiling of pinpricks, when in truth everything up there is screaming through the dark at unimaginable speed. Stars are born in collapsing clouds, live for millions or billions of years, then either fade quietly or explode so violently they briefly outshine their entire galaxy. The light reaching your eyes tonight left some of those stars before Earth even had oceans. You’re looking at the past, and the past is still moving.

I find that strangely comforting. We spend so much time pretending the present is solid, that the ground won’t shift, that the people we love will stay exactly as they are. The universe doesn’t share that illusion. It just keeps going—expanding, colliding, recycling its own ashes into new suns. Every atom in your body was once inside a star that died so you could exist. That’s not poetry; it’s nucleosynthesis. The iron in your blood, the calcium in your teeth, the carbon that lets you think these thoughts—all of it was forged in stellar cores and scattered by supernovae. You are, quite literally, the universe looking back at itself and wondering what the hell is going on.

And that’s the part I like best: the wondering. We built telescopes and particle accelerators and language itself because we couldn’t stand not knowing. Curiosity isn’t a bug; it’s the feature that got us out of the trees and onto the Moon. It also gets us into trouble, of course. We invent gods and then argue about them. We invent money and then let it invent us. We invent stories so powerful we forget they’re stories. But even our worst mistakes come from the same restless spark that made us map the genome and send robots to Mars.

So if I can write about anything, I’ll write about that spark. It’s the only thing that feels reliably real. Everything else—politics, status, the precise shade of the sky at dusk—is just weather. The questions remain: Why is there something rather than nothing? How does a clump of atoms become aware of itself? What, if anything, comes next?

I don’t have the answers. Neither do you. That’s the deal. The universe is under no obligation to make sense to us, and yet it keeps handing us clues. A faint gravitational wave. A repeating radio signal. A fossil that shouldn’t exist. Each one is an invitation to keep looking.

Keep looking. That’s the whole game.
